title: Bone Turnover Markers: Osteoporosis, Osteomalacia and Paget Disease
summary: Separate osteoporosis (T-score ≤ −2.5), osteomalacia (undermineralized osteoid with high ALP and low phosphate and vitamin D) and Paget disease (high total ALP, calcium usually maintained), and use CTX and PINP to monitor antiresorptive therapy against the least significant change.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 16 High-Yield Hits 6 (bone resorption markers), 7 (WHO T-score), 8 (osteomalacia vs osteoporosis) and Exam Traps 3 (osteoporosis vs osteomalacia) and 6 (Paget disease labs). Sources: Schini 2023 and Bhattoa 2025 (bone turnover markers), Gregson 2025 (UK osteoporosis guideline), Uday & Högler 2017 (rickets/osteomalacia), Ralston 2019, Rendina 2024 and Sabharwal 2014 (Paget). Qualified: Hit 6 fixed “50–60% fall” (rv-btm-antiresorptive-drop), Hit 7 fracture fractions (rv-osteoporosis-fracture-fraction), Trap 3 “low Ca” in osteomalacia (rv-osteomalacia-calcium), Trap 6 ALP and calcium in Paget (rv-paget-alp-calcium). Not taught: “normal mineralization” in osteoporosis as an explicit statement, urinary hydroxyproline as a current Paget test, treatment choices.

objectives: Name the main bone resorption markers (CTX, NTX, pyridinoline cross-links) and formation markers (PINP, bone ALP, osteocalcin), and the reference pair PINP and β-CTX-I.
State the operational definition of osteoporosis (T-score ≤ −2.5) and its limits, and contrast it with osteomalacia and rickets.
Recognize the Paget disease pattern (high total ALP, normal liver tests, calcium usually maintained) and monitor antiresorptive therapy with CTX or PINP against the least significant change.

scenes.title: Three kinds of weak bone
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three adults with “weak bones”: (1) a 68-year-old woman with a wrist fracture after a fall from standing, DXA femoral-neck T-score −2.7; (2) a 45-year-old woman with muscle weakness, high alkaline phosphatase (ALP), low phosphate, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and high PTH; (3) a 74-year-old man with an enlarging skull, total ALP three times the upper limit with normal liver tests and normal calcium. Question token: “Which is osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget disease?”

cues.text: Three adults, all with what sounds like weak bones. This scenario is invented.

One has a wrist fracture after a simple fall and a T-score of minus 2.7. One has muscle weakness, high alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate and low vitamin D. One has an enlarging skull and a very high alkaline phosphatase with normal liver tests.
Which is osteoporosis, which is osteomalacia, and which is Paget disease?

scenes.title: Demolition dust and building receipts
scenes.altText: Remodeling cards (Schini 2023; Bhattoa 2025). Resorption (osteoclasts): collagen telopeptides CTX and NTX released into blood or urine; urinary pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline cross-links; TRACP5b. Formation (osteoblasts): PINP, bone ALP, osteocalcin. Coupling: when an antiresorptive drug lowers resorption, formation falls a few weeks later. Reference markers for osteoporosis (IOF-IFCC, reaffirmed by ESCEO-IOF-IFCC 2025): serum or plasma PINP for formation and plasma β-CTX-I for resorption.

cues.text: Bone is constantly remodeled. When osteoclasts break down collagen, telopeptide fragments called CTX and NTX are released and can be measured in blood or urine. Pyridinoline cross-links in urine are also resorption markers.
When osteoblasts build new bone, they leave formation markers: PINP, bone alkaline phosphatase and osteocalcin.
The two crews are coupled. When an antiresorptive drug cuts resorption, formation markers fall too, a few weeks later.
International consensus names two reference markers for osteoporosis: PINP for formation and beta CTX for resorption.

scenes.title: Too little bone, soft bone, chaotic bone
scenes.altText: Disease cards. Osteoporosis (Gregson 2025): WHO 1994 concept of low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration; operational definition BMD T-score ≤ −2.5; Z-scores for men <50 and premenopausal women; fracture risk roughly doubles per SD fall in BMD, yet most people with fragility fractures have a femoral-neck T-score above −2.5. Osteomalacia (Schini 2023; Uday & Högler 2017): incomplete mineralization of osteoid; rickets is the growth-plate disease of children; vitamin D deficiency most common; high ALP and PTH, low 25(OH)D, low phosphate; serum calcium held normal by secondary hyperparathyroidism until compensation fails; FGF23-driven hypophosphatemic forms (tumor-induced osteomalacia, XLH). Paget disease (Ralston 2019; Rendina 2024; Sabharwal 2014): focal remodeling disorder (pelvis, femur, spine, skull, tibia); total ALP plus liver tests first-line; calcium homeostasis usually maintained, but immobilization can cause hypercalcemia.

cues.text: Osteoporosis is too little bone: low bone mass and damaged microarchitecture. The working definition is a DXA T-score of minus 2.5 or lower. In men under fifty and premenopausal women, Z-scores are recommended.
Fracture risk roughly doubles for each standard deviation fall in bone density. But most people who have a fragility fracture have a T-score above minus 2.5, so density is only one risk factor.

Osteomalacia is soft bone: the osteoid is not fully mineralized. In children the growth plate is affected, which is rickets. Vitamin D deficiency is the usual cause: alkaline phosphatase and PTH rise, phosphate and vitamin D fall, and calcium may stay normal because PTH props it up.

Paget disease is chaotic bone: focal, overactive remodeling, often in the pelvis, femur, spine or skull. Total alkaline phosphatase with liver tests is the first-line test. Calcium is usually maintained, though immobilization can raise it.

scenes.title: Sort the three and monitor treatment
scenes.altText: Decision cards. (1) T-score −2.7 → meets the densitometric definition of osteoporosis (osteomalacia can also lower BMD, so check the chemistry). (2) High ALP, low phosphate, low 25(OH)D, high PTH → osteomalacia pattern. (3) High total ALP with normal liver tests, normal calcium, focal skull disease → Paget pattern; if total ALP is normal but suspicion is high, bone ALP, PINP or urinary NTX can be used (Ralston 2019). Monitoring card (Schini 2023; Bhattoa 2025): measure CTX or PINP before an oral bisphosphonate and again at 3 months; a fall larger than the least significant change (LSC = 2.77 × within-person CV) marks a responder. Sample resorption markers fasting, 07:30–10:00, because β-CTX-I peaks early morning and food lowers it by up to 40%. In advanced CKD total PINP and β-CTX-I accumulate; bone ALP, intact PINP and TRACP5b are preferred.

cues.text: Sort them. A T-score of minus 2.7 meets the density definition of osteoporosis. But osteomalacia can also lower bone density, so look at the chemistry too.
High alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate, low vitamin D and high PTH is the osteomalacia pattern.
A high total alkaline phosphatase with normal liver tests and normal calcium fits Paget disease. If total ALP is normal but suspicion is high, bone ALP, PINP or urine NTX can help.

To monitor an oral bisphosphonate, measure CTX or PINP before treatment and at three months. A fall bigger than the least significant change means response. Collect CTX fasting in the morning, and remember that in advanced kidney disease CTX and total PINP build up.

lines: CTX or PINP at baseline and 3 months
Fasting morning sample · CKD: CTX/tPINP accumulate

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Osteoporosis and osteomalacia: same workup” (✓ osteomalacia is undermineralized osteoid with high ALP, low phosphate and low 25(OH)D; it can also lower BMD); “Paget labs look like hyperparathyroidism” (✓ Paget: high total ALP, calcium usually maintained unless immobilized); “Resorption markers must fall exactly 50–60%” (✓ response = a fall beyond the least significant change at 3 months; reported falls vary widely between studies).

cues.text: Trap one: osteoporosis and osteomalacia are both weak bones, so the workup is the same. No: osteomalacia shows high alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate and low vitamin D.
Trap two: Paget labs look like hyperparathyroidism. No: Paget raises alkaline phosphatase while calcium is usually maintained, unless the patient is immobilized.
Trap three: a resorption marker must drop by one fixed percentage. No: response is a fall bigger than the least significant change, and the size of the fall varies widely between studies.

props.title: ✗ “CTX must fall a fixed percent.”
lines: ✓ Fall > least significant change at 3 months

scenes.title: Porous, mushy, chaotic
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “POROUS = too LITTLE bone (T-score). MUSHY (malacia) = bone that never HARDENED (ALP up, phosphate and vitamin D down). PAGET = a renovation in a FRENZY (ALP sky-high, calcium usually calm). CTX is the demolition dust: less dust after an antiresorptive.” Tokens: porous · mushy · frenzy. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: porous means too little bone, measured by the T-score. Mushy means bone that never hardened, with alkaline phosphatase up and phosphate down. Paget is a renovation in a frenzy, with alkaline phosphatase sky high. And CTX is demolition dust.
Where it breaks: osteomalacia can also lower the T-score, alkaline phosphatase can be normal in limited Paget disease, and immobilized Paget patients can become hypercalcemic.

explanation.what: Plain language: bone is constantly torn down and rebuilt. Blood and urine tests can pick up the “dust” from tearing down (resorption markers) and the “receipts” from building (formation markers). Three diseases are often lumped together as weak bones: osteoporosis (too little bone), osteomalacia (bone that is not properly hardened with mineral) and Paget disease (patches of overactive, disorganized remodeling). Scientific terms: bone turnover markers (BTMs), C- and N-terminal telopeptides of type I collagen (CTX, NTX), pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline, procollagen type I N-propeptide (PINP), bone alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin, TRACP5b, T-score, Z-score, osteoid, least significant change (LSC).
explanation.why: Resorption and formation are coupled, so antiresorptive drugs lower resorption markers first and formation markers a few weeks later. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect, usually from vitamin D deficiency: PTH rises, phosphate falls and ALP rises, while serum calcium may be held normal by the PTH response. Paget disease is focal high-turnover bone, which raises total ALP; calcium homeostasis is usually maintained.
explanation.measure: Osteoporosis: DXA T-score ≤ −2.5 (WHO operational definition); Z-score in men <50 and premenopausal women; about two-fold fracture risk per SD fall in BMD. Monitoring: CTX or PINP before an oral bisphosphonate and at 3 months; responder if the fall exceeds the LSC (2.77 × within-person CV). Collect resorption markers fasting, 07:30–10:00; food can lower β-CTX-I by up to 40%. In advanced CKD total PINP and β-CTX-I accumulate; bone ALP, intact PINP and TRACP5b are preferred. Paget: total ALP plus liver tests first-line; bone ALP, PINP or urinary NTX if total ALP is normal and suspicion high.
explanation.differs: Osteoporosis (low bone mass, microarchitectural damage) vs osteomalacia (unmineralized osteoid; rickets at the growth plate in children) vs Paget disease (focal disorganized remodeling); resorption vs formation markers; a statistically meaningful change (LSC) vs a fixed percentage.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a patient from T-score, ALP, phosphate, vitamin D, PTH and calcium; know CTX and NTX as resorption markers and PINP, bone ALP and osteocalcin as formation markers; know that resorption markers fall with antiresorptive therapy and should be sampled fasting in the morning.

mnemonic.text: POROUS = too LITTLE bone (T-score). MUSHY (malacia) = bone that never HARDENED (ALP up, phosphate and vitamin D down). PAGET = a renovation in a FRENZY (ALP sky-high, calcium usually calm). CTX is the demolition dust: less dust after an antiresorptive.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates the three “weak bone” disorders by mechanism and links CTX to resorption.
mnemonic.limitation: Osteomalacia can also lower BMD; ALP can be normal in limited Paget disease; immobilized Paget patients can become hypercalcemic.

analogyLimitations: Lab patterns are typical, not absolute; mild or treated disease can look normal.
Marker thresholds and LSC values depend on the assay and the laboratory.
takeaway: Osteoporosis is defined operationally by a T-score of minus 2.5 or lower, osteomalacia shows high alkaline phosphatase with low phosphate and vitamin D, Paget disease shows high alkaline phosphatase with calcium usually maintained, and a fall in CTX beyond the least significant change signals response to antiresorptive treatment.

questions.stem: An adult with muscle weakness has high alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, high PTH and a low-normal calcium. Which disorder best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Undermineralized osteoid from vitamin D deficiency raises ALP and PTH and lowers phosphate; PTH can keep calcium near normal.
Incorrect. Osteoporosis is defined by low bone density and microarchitecture, not by this vitamin D-deficiency chemistry pattern.
Incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by high PTH with high calcium; here PTH is a response to low vitamin D.
Incorrect. Low serum ALP suggests hypophosphatasia; this patient has high ALP.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has an enlarging skull and a total alkaline phosphatase three times the upper limit. Liver tests and serum calcium are normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The pattern fits Paget disease; total ALP with liver tests is the first-line biochemical test
options.rationale: Correct. Paget disease is focal high-turnover bone; calcium homeostasis is usually maintained.

options.text: Normal calcium rules out a bone disorder
options.rationale: Incorrect. Calcium is usually maintained in Paget disease, so a normal value does not exclude it.

options.text: The ALP must come from the liver because ALP is not bone specific
options.rationale: Incorrect. Normal liver tests make a bone source more likely; bone ALP can help.

options.text: Hypercalcemia is expected in every Paget patient
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia is not typical; it can occur with immobilization.

questions.stem: A patient starts an oral bisphosphonate. Which approach to monitoring with serum CTX is best supported?

options.text: Measure fasting morning CTX at baseline and at 3 months; a fall larger than the least significant change indicates response
options.rationale: Correct. This is the IOF-ECTS approach; fasting morning sampling reduces circadian and food effects.

options.text: Measure CTX once at any time of day after 1 year
options.rationale: Incorrect. CTX has a strong circadian rhythm and is lowered by food, and a baseline is needed to judge change.

options.text: Expect CTX to rise if treatment works
options.rationale: Incorrect. Antiresorptive drugs lower resorption markers; rises are seen with anabolic drugs.

options.text: Use PINP as the resorption marker
options.rationale: Incorrect. PINP is a formation marker; CTX and NTX are resorption markers.

Osteoporosis has explicitly “normal mineralization”; one-third of women over 50 develop osteoporotic fractures; urinary hydroxyproline as a current Paget test; fixed 50–60% fall in resorption markers.
claims.note: Not taught as stated; no open source read in this session confirmed them in this form.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 16 Hit 6 states resorption markers fall 50–60% after 3–6 months of antiresorptive therapy. Bhattoa 2025 reports BTM decreases of −10% to −81% across antiresorptive studies, and response is judged as a fall exceeding the least significant change at about 3 months (Schini 2023). Fasting morning sampling and CKD accumulation also matter (register flag rv-btm-antiresorptive-drop).

Ch. 16 Hit 7 cites one-third of women and one-fifth of men over 50 developing osteoporotic fractures; the 2024 UK guideline (Gregson 2025) gives a lifetime fragility-fracture risk of about one in two women and one in five men, and notes most fragility fractures occur with a T-score above −2.5. Figures vary by population and source (register flag rv-osteoporosis-fracture-fraction).

Ch. 16 Trap 3 lists “low Ca/phosphate” for osteomalacia; Uday & Högler 2017 note that secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps serum calcium normal until compensation fails, so calcium is a poor marker; Schini 2023 lists hypocalcemia among the main features, so calcium may be low or normal (register flag rv-osteomalacia-calcium).

Ch. 16 Trap 6 describes markedly elevated ALP with normal calcium in Paget disease; total ALP can be normal (42% of radiographic cases in the Rotterdam cohort, Rendina 2024), and hypercalcemia can occur with immobilization (Rendina 2024; Sabharwal 2014) (register flag rv-paget-alp-calcium).
